section.title: Epilogue
section.sectionRationale: This closing unit functions as the epilogue not only of Revelation but, canonically, of the entire Christian Bible. The angel authenticates the whole vision as faithful and true, John's premature worship of the angel is corrected with 'Worship God,' Jesus speaks in the first person three times promising to come soon, a solemn warning is issued against tampering with the prophecy, and the book closes with the church's ancient prayer, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' and a benediction of grace. It is bounded by the angel's opening authentication in verse 6 and the grace-benediction that ends the whole book in verse 21.
section.thesis: The Lord who has shown these true and faithful words is coming soon; His people are to keep, not alter, this prophecy, to wash their robes, and to answer His promise with the church's ancient prayer, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' resting in His grace until He does.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the angel's authentication of the prophecy and the blessing on those who keep it; John's misdirected worship of the angel and the correction, 'Worship God'; Jesus' declaration, 'I am coming soon,' with His reward and the final either/or of blessing or exclusion; His self-testimony as the Root and Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star, and the Spirit and the bride's invitation to come; and the closing warning against adding to or taking from the prophecy, the prayer 'Come, Lord Jesus,' and the benediction of grace.

units.label: These words are faithful and true

verses.text: Then the angel said to me, “These words are faithful and true. The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent His angel to show His servants what must {{tachy|soon}} take place.”
“Behold, I am coming {{tachy|soon}}. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book.”
And I am John, who heard and saw these things. And when I had heard and seen them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who had shown me these things.
But he said to me, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!”
Then he told me, “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near.
Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous, and the vile continue to be vile; let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and the holy continue to be holy.”

units.label: I am coming soon, with My reward

verses.text: “Behold, I am coming {{tachy|soon}}, and My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.”
Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates.
But outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.

units.label: The Root and Offspring of David, the Morning Star
units.note: Jesus' own testimony, and the invitation to come

verses.text: “I, Jesus, have sent My angel to give you this testimony for the churches. I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright {{aster_proinos|Morning Star}}.”
The Spirit and the bride say, “{{erchou|Come}}!” Let the one who hears say, “{{erchou|Come}}!” And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.

units.label: The warning, the prayer, and the benediction
units.note: do not add or take away; Come, Lord Jesus

verses.text: I testify to everyone who hears the words of prophecy in this book: If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book.
And if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book.
He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am {{tachy|coming soon}}.” Amen. {{erchou|Come}}, Lord Jesus!
The {{charis|grace}} of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen.

tachy.gloss: Quickly, soon, with speed. Used three times in this chapter of Christ's coming, it is debated whether it names calendar nearness or the suddenness and certainty of the event once it begins; either sense presses believers toward constant, watchful readiness rather than complacency.

aster_proinos.gloss: The Morning Star, the bright star that heralds the dawn. Jesus takes this title for Himself, fulfilling the star that would rise out of Jacob, Numbers 24:17, and named again as a sign of certain hope in 2 Peter 1:19.

erchou.gloss: Come, an imperative from erchomai, to come or go. It is the Spirit and the bride's invitation, the hearer's echo of it, and finally the church's own prayer addressed to the returning Christ, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' in verse 20.

charis.gloss: Grace, unmerited favor. It is the very last word given for the whole book of Revelation, and by canonical placement, the closing note of the entire Christian Bible, a fitting seal on a book so full of warning and wonder.

basic.context: The angel closes the vision by insisting every word of it is faithful and true. John is so overwhelmed he falls down to worship the angel, but is corrected at once, 'Worship God.' Jesus then speaks directly three times, promising 'I am coming soon,' before the book ends with a warning not to tamper with its words and the church's prayer, 'Come, Lord Jesus.'
basic.hermeneutics: Readers debate what 'soon' means after two thousand years, some reading it as imminent readiness for every generation, others as prophetic language about the suddenness of the event rather than its calendar timing. Either way, the text calls for watchful, faithful living now, not date-setting.
basic.originalLanguages: Christ says He is coming tachy, soon or swiftly, three times. He calls Himself the Morning Star, aster ho proinos, the herald of the dawn. The Spirit and the bride cry erchou, Come, and the whole book ends on charis, grace, its very last word.
basic.typology: The tree of life and the holy city, once barred from fallen humanity, are now freely promised to those who wash their robes. The warning against adding to or removing from this book echoes Moses' warning about the Law, and the prayer 'Come, Lord Jesus' echoes the ancient Aramaic cry Maranatha.
basic.christ: Jesus speaks in the first person, 'I, Jesus,' naming Himself Root and Offspring of David and the bright Morning Star, both fully divine and truly human, David's Lord and David's descendant, promising to come soon and to reward each according to what has been done.
basic.god: God is the God of the spirits of the prophets who sent His angel, whose words are faithful and true, who warns against tampering with them, and whose grace is the very last word of the whole Bible.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32 warn against adding to or taking from God's word. Numbers 24:17 and Isaiah 11:1, 10 promise the Star and Root of David. 1 Corinthians 16:22 preserves the same prayer in Aramaic, Maranatha, Come, our Lord.
basic.oneStory: The Bible that began with humanity barred from the tree of life by a flaming sword ends with an open invitation, 'Come,' and the tree of life freely promised to those who wash their robes, sealed by the grace of the Lord Jesus and the church's ancient prayer for His return.

context.literary:
The epilogue is a rapid exchange of voices, and part of its force is that the reader cannot always tell who is speaking. The angel speaks in verse 6, and then, without a marker, Jesus in verse 7, 'Behold, I am coming soon.' John names himself in verse 8, the angel returns in verses 9 to 11, and the voice of Jesus breaks in again at verses 12 to 13 and 16. The Spirit and the bride speak in verse 17, a warning is attached in verses 18 to 19 as a solemn testimony, and in verse 20 Jesus answers 'Yes, I am coming soon' and John answers 'Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!' The blur of speakers is deliberate. The angel's words, Christ's words and the prophet's words are presented as one message that carries the authority of its source.

The closing is a deliberate mirror of the opening. Revelation 1:1 spoke of 'what must soon come to pass' made known by an angel to John, and 22:6 repeats nearly the same phrase. The blessing on the one who reads and keeps the words, 1:3, returns in 22:7. 'The time is near,' 1:3, returns as 22:10. The Alpha and the Omega of 1:8 speaks again in 22:13, the 'Amen' of 1:7 is repeated in 22:20, and the grace of 1:4 closes the book in 22:21. The book is set within a frame, and so what lies between is to be read as a letter to the churches, with an opening and a closing as a letter has.

The beatitudes are another thread. Revelation contains seven blessings, at 1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7 and 22:14, and the last two are in this section. The first tells the reader to keep the words, and the last tells the reader to wash the robes. The scene of the angel and the worship in verses 8 and 9 reproduces the scene of 19:9-10 almost exactly, and the repeat is part of the lesson: even a seer who has seen so much can still bow to the wrong person.
context.historical:
The first hearers were Christians in the Roman province of Asia, living under real pressure and waiting for Christ's return, and what stood between them and any other loyalty was the word 'Lord.' The empire asked its subjects to give that title to Caesar, and the churches confessed it of Jesus. A book that closes with 'Come, Lord Jesus' is a book that has chosen its master. The prayer itself was not invented for Greek speakers. The Aramaic form, Maranatha, appears untranslated in the Greek letter of 1 Corinthians 16:22, and an early church manual called the Didache also preserves it in its prayers, which shows how deeply the cry was rooted in the first Christian worship.

The command 'Do not seal up' in verse 10 is deliberate contrast with Daniel. Daniel was told to 'shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end,' Daniel 12:4 and 12:9, because the end lay far off. John is told that the book is to stay open, since 'the time is near.' The prophecy is meant to be read in public in the churches, as 1:3 says. The warning against adding or taking away is also at home in the ancient world, where law codes and treaties often closed with curses on anyone who altered them. Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32 do the same for the law, and Proverbs 30:5-6 for the words of God.

The list outside the city in verse 15 would have sounded familiar to people in Ephesus and the cities nearby. Sorcery was a trade there, and Acts 19:19 records a pile of magic books burned in public. 'Dogs' were scavengers and a standard insult, and Paul uses the word for false teachers in Philippians 3:2. The names for Jesus would have carried weight too. The 'bright Morning Star' could recall the star that Balaam saw rising from Jacob, Numbers 24:17, which Israel read as a coming king, and 'the Root and the Offspring of David' is the title of a promised heir.
context.canonical:
This is the last page of the Christian Bible, and it works as a closing for the whole canon as well as for the book. The tree of life, which was barred to Adam and Eve at Genesis 3:24, is now offered to those who wash their robes, verse 14. The word of God, which began with 'Let there be light,' ends with the Lord God as the light of His people, 22:5. The first book has a serpent and a curse, and the last has a promise that the curse is gone and that the ancient serpent, named in 12:9 and 20:10, has been dealt with.

The Old Testament speaks through nearly every phrase. 'The God of the spirits of the prophets' echoes the title 'the God of the spirits of all flesh,' Numbers 16:22 and 27:16. The Morning Star is from Numbers 24:17, and the Root is from Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10. The invitation to the thirsty comes from Isaiah 55:1, 'Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters.' The reward 'with Me' repeats Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11, where the coming LORD brings His recompense with Him. The warning against changing the book is the shadow of Deuteronomy 4:2.

The New Testament speaks of the same hope in many voices. Jesus said, 'I will come back and welcome you into My presence,' John 14:3, and the angels at the ascension said that the same Jesus 'will come back in the same way,' Acts 1:11. Paul calls it 'the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,' Titus 2:13, and Hebrews says that 'In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay,' Hebrews 10:37. Jesus' own warning to stay awake, Matthew 24:42-44, is picked up at Revelation 16:15, and the prayer of 22:20 is the church's answer to all of them. The grace with which the book ends is the grace with which Paul closed his letters, Romans 16:20 and 2 Corinthians 13:14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John closes the book as a pastor. He has shown the churches a great deal, and he must now say what they are to do with it. The first task is to trust it. The angel states twice that these words are 'faithful and true,' and the God who sent the angel is the God of the prophets, so the book belongs among the prophets and not among the speculations of the age. The second is to keep it, which in the Bible's language is more than reading. It means holding to it and obeying it, and the blessing of verse 7 goes to the one who does.

John also means to correct a particular failing, the temptation to worship what is wonderful rather than the One who sent it. If the seer himself can fall at the angel's feet, the readers are in danger too. The angel's reply, 'Worship God!', is a summary of the book's whole purpose. The beast is worshipped by the world, and God alone is worthy.

And John intends to turn the whole vision into a prayer. The Spirit and the bride say 'Come,' the hearer is told to say 'Come,' and the thirsty are told to come. The warning in verses 18 and 19 guards the words so that they will not be softened to fit the age, and the final benediction places the readers under grace, since no one can wash a robe or keep a word without it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The epilogue mixes description and command with unusual closeness. It describes Christ's coming, His reward, the exclusion of the wicked and the invitation of the thirsty, and it prescribes worship of God alone, keeping the words, washing the robes, and praying for His coming. Every command rests on a promise.

Two cautions are worth stating. The sentence 'Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous,' verse 11, is not a command to do wrong. It is a stark description of the fixed state that waits when the time is up, and it is spoken to make the hearer feel the urgency of turning now. And the warning of verses 18 and 19 is a protection for this book, written in the form that Moses used for the law. It does not tell believers to avoid translation, interpretation or application, or to refuse every later writer. It tells them not to alter, soften or invent what God has said.

The statement that Christ is coming soon is meant to be received with watchfulness and not with a stopwatch. Jesus Himself said that no one knows the day, Matthew 24:42-44, and Paul told the Thessalonians not to be alarmed by claims that the day has already come, 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3. Setting dates is the opposite of the prayer of verse 20.

debates.question: In what sense is Jesus 'coming soon,' Revelation 22:7, 12, 20, given that two thousand years have passed?

views.label: 'Soon' as genuine nearness, calling every generation to live in readiness
views.case: The New Testament treats the return as always near. Jesus said to stay awake because the hour is unknown, Matthew 24:42-44, and Revelation 3:11 and 16:15 attach the same urgency to watchfulness. On this view 'soon' names the posture believers must keep, and it is true in every generation.

views.label: 'Soon' as prophetic idiom for suddenness and certainty
views.case: The Greek word tachy can mean quickly as well as soon, as the BSB footnote on 22:6 allows ('suddenly or quickly'). On this view the stress falls on how swiftly the event comes once it begins, and 2 Peter 3:8-9 reminds readers that the Lord's delay is patience, with a day like a thousand years, so the lapse of time does not contradict the promise.

views.label: 'Soon' as near for the first readers in the events that start the process
views.case: Those who read much of the book as pointing to the pressures of the first century, such as persecution and the pull of Rome, take 'soon' and 'the time is near' literally for John's readers. The first hearers would see the opening movements of the conflict, and the end would follow the same pattern.

debates.bearing: All three views hold that the promise is true and that the right response is readiness and not date-setting. The book itself pairs the word 'soon' with 'Come, Lord Jesus,' so the question is first a matter of prayer and then a matter of calculation.

debates.question: What do the warnings of verses 18 and 19 protect, and who do they bind?

views.label: This book alone
views.case: The words say 'the words of the prophecy of this book,' and they follow a pattern from Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32, which protected the law of Moses and not other texts. Revelation was written first as a letter, and the warning means that the churches must not alter the letter before them.

views.label: The whole canon, as the last book
views.case: Since Revelation stands last, many in the church have heard it as a seal on the whole of Scripture. The point is not that it was written last in time, but that it stands last in the canon, and that the pattern of Proverbs 30:5-6 applies to every word of God, and so the principle reaches beyond this book.

views.label: The loss of a share is a warning about character, not a bare penalty
views.case: Some stress that the punishments, plagues and loss of 'his share in the tree of life,' suit someone who deliberately twists the message, as in 2 Peter 3:16, and not a sincere believer who struggles with a hard text. They point out that the warning follows the verses about those outside, who 'love and practice falsehood,' 22:15.

debates.bearing: The passage does not ban interpretation, since the angel commands the book to be read, heard and kept. It forbids falsifying the word. The call is to hold the text as given and to apply it faithfully.

study.originalLanguages:
Three verbs shape the epilogue. The first is tereo, 'to keep,' in 22:7 and 22:9, the same verb as the blessing in 1:3 and one that means to guard and to obey, as a sentry guards a post. The blessing is on the one who keeps the words, and the angel counts himself among 'those who keep the words of this book.' The second is proskyneo, 'to worship,' in 22:8, which is literally to fall down and kiss the ground in homage. The angel's answer, 'Worship God,' uses the same verb as an imperative. The third is erchou, 'Come,' the imperative of erchomai, in 22:17 and 22:20. In verse 17 the Spirit and the bride speak it to the Lord, and in the same verse the hearer is told to say it and the thirsty are told to come, which is a different construction, a third person command 'let him come.' The book ends with a single word used in three directions, as a prayer for Christ to come, as an invitation to the hearer, and as a call to the thirsty.

The title of verse 16, 'the Root and the Offspring of David,' joins two Greek words, riza and genos. Riza is a root, a source, and genos is offspring, family or race. He is the source from which David came and the descendant who came from David. The words 'Morning Star' are aster ho proinos, 'the star, the early one,' the one that shines before the sun. The adjective proinos belongs to the morning, and Jesus offers the same star to the overcomer in 2:28.

The wording of verse 14 has a notable textual twist. The BSB reads 'Blessed are those who wash their robes,' and its footnote says that the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read instead 'Blessed are those who do His commandments.' The two phrases look alike in Greek, plynontes tas stolas against poiountes tas entolas, which makes a scribal slip easy to imagine. The earlier reading uses a present participle, 'washing,' and recalls 7:14, where the robes were washed in the blood of the Lamb. The word for 'right,' exousia, means authority or permission, and it makes the access a granted privilege.

The list of verse 15 begins with kynes, 'dogs,' and includes pharmakoi, 'sorcerers,' whose word is related to drugs and potions, and ends with everyone who 'loves and practices falsehood,' the Greek pairing philon kai poion pseudos, 'loving and doing a lie.' The pairing of loving and doing names both the heart and the hand. Verse 9 calls the angel a syndoulos, a fellow slave, which puts the seer, the prophets and the angel on the same level before God, and the same word appears at 19:10.

The last word of the book is charis, 'grace.' The footnote to 22:21 shows that manuscripts differ at the end, some having 'with all the saints,' some 'with all,' and some lacking 'Amen,' but they all end with charis, and so the book ends as Paul's letters do, in grace.

typology.type: The tree of life offered to the washed, Genesis 3:24
typology.fulfillment: Cherubim and a whirling sword guarded the way to the tree of life, and Adam and Eve were driven out. Revelation 22:14 gives the right to the tree and entry to the city to those who wash their robes. Zechariah 3:3-5 had pictured the high priest Joshua in filthy clothes, who was given clean garments by God, and Revelation 7:14 says the robes are made white in the blood of the Lamb. The escalation is that the door is opened by the Lamb and not by the worth of the one who enters. The type falls short in that Eden's tree could be forfeited, while this access is for those whose names are in the Lamb's book.

typology.type: Moses' warning about the law, Deuteronomy 4:2
typology.fulfillment: Moses told Israel, 'You must not add to or subtract from what I command you,' and repeated it at Deuteronomy 12:32. John uses the same shape for the prophecy of this book, with plagues for adding and the loss of a share in the tree of life for taking away. The parallel marks Revelation as the word of God in the same sense as the law. The correspondence is deliberate and complete in form, but it differs in its penalty, since Moses speaks of keeping the commandments, and John names the very tree of life from which Adam was barred.

typology.type: The star out of Jacob, Numbers 24:17
typology.fulfillment: Balaam saw a star come forth from Jacob and a scepter rise from Israel, and the Jews took it as a promise of a king. Jesus says in Revelation 22:16 that He is the bright Morning Star, and in 2:28 He promises to give the morning star to the overcomer. The Magi saw 'His star in the east,' Matthew 2:2, and Zechariah's song speaks of 'the Dawn' that will visit from on high, Luke 1:78. The escalation is from a distant king to a Lord who is the dawn itself, and who shares His glory with His people. The type falls short in that a star only announces day, while He is the one who brings the unending day of 22:5.

typology.type: The Root of Jesse and the Davidic king, Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foresaw a Branch from the stump of Jesse and, in 11:10, 'the Root of Jesse' who will stand as a banner for the peoples, so that the nations seek Him. Revelation 5:5 calls the Lamb 'the Root of David,' and 22:16 adds 'the Offspring of David.' Jesus pressed the puzzle in Matthew 22:41-45, asking how David could call his own son 'Lord.' The answer is that He is both. The correspondence holds in His full humanity and His eternal lordship, and it falls short of every earlier Davidic king, who were only offspring and never the root.

Isaiah called, 'Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters,' and the invitation was free. In John 7:37 Jesus stood and called out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink.' Revelation 22:17 makes it the last invitation in the Bible, and gives the water to anyone who desires it, 'drink freely.' The escalation is that the one who is calling is the One who gives the water, and the call now carries the Spirit and the bride. The type falls short in that Isaiah's water was an image of covenant blessings, while this water flows from the throne itself, as in 22:1.

study.christ:
In this closing scene Jesus speaks in His own voice again, as He did in the letters to the churches. 'I am coming soon' stands at verses 7, 12 and 20, and in verse 16 He introduces Himself by His personal name, 'I, Jesus.' The vision that began as 'the revelation of Jesus Christ,' 1:1, ends with Him vouching for it Himself. He sent the angel, He gives the testimony, and He answers the church's prayer with 'Yes.'

His title in verse 13, 'the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End,' is a stacking of three titles, and each belongs to God. The first and the last is God's title in Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12, and the Alpha and the Omega is the Lord God's in Revelation 1:8 and 21:6. Jesus took 'the First and the Last' for Himself in 1:17 and 2:8. In 22:13 all three are gathered and spoken by Him, so that the Lord who is coming is the Lord who made all things and will end all things. The reward 'with Me' in verse 12 is a divine promise. Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 said that the LORD's reward was with Him when He came, and now Jesus says it of Himself. So is the right to give to 'each one according to what he has done,' since the Father 'has assigned all judgment to the Son,' John 5:22.

The title in verse 16 holds His person together. As the Root of David He is the source from which David came, and as the Offspring of David He is his descendant, and so He is both David's Lord and David's son, the puzzle He set in Matthew 22:41-45 on the strength of Psalm 110:1. As the Morning Star He is the one who ends the night. Numbers 24:17 spoke of the star out of Jacob, and Peter spoke of the morning star rising in the heart, 2 Peter 1:19.

The worship of the passage is also telling. The angel refuses worship, 'Worship God!' But the book has already shown the Lamb receiving it, together with the One on the throne, Revelation 5:8 and 5:13. The same book that forbids bowing to a creature allows bowing to the Lamb, and that is only coherent if the Lamb is on the God side of that line.

The last line is the benediction, 'The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints.' The whole Bible ends with His name and His grace. Reading Jesus into every detail would be a mistake, but here He speaks for Himself, and the text does not ask the reader to find Him between the lines.
study.god:
The God of this passage is named in verse 6 as 'the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets,' which recalls Moses' title 'the God of the spirits of all flesh,' Numbers 16:22 and 27:16. He is the Lord who governs the inner life of every person and who has spoken through every true prophet. The word the angel brings is therefore not the opinion of a seer but the speech of the God who made the minds that receive it. That is the ground of the angel's repeated assurance that the words are 'faithful and true,' since God cannot deny what He has said.

He is a God who sends. He sends His angel, and Jesus sends His angel for the churches, so that the message goes out from God by a chosen messenger to a chosen people. He is also a God who keeps His own word safe. The warning against adding or taking away means that what He says is not ours to edit. It matches the care of Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:5-6, 'Every word of God is flawless.' A God who is truth cannot be represented by invented words.

He is the only one to be worshiped, and the angel's rebuke is the plainest statement of that in the book. This is a doctrine of God as much as a command: God alone is the final object of human devotion, and no creature, however glorious, may take the place. Revelation 4:11 grounds it in creation, 'for You created all things.'

He is just and gives to each according to what he has done, and He is patient. The coming is 'soon,' and yet 2 Peter 3:9 says that the Lord is 'not slow in keeping His promise' but is 'patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish.' The offer remains open to the thirsty, 'drink freely,' and the same God who bars the unclean calls them to wash. This is the pattern of Exodus 34:6, a God who is compassionate and gracious, and who does not leave the guilty unpunished.

He is the God of grace. The book closes with a blessing and not a threat, 'The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints,' and the last word is charis. For worship, this passage teaches believers to receive God's word with reverence, to bow to Him alone, to answer His promise with prayer, and to rest in the grace that holds them until He comes.

crossReferences.note: The opening of the book is the other half of the frame. It speaks of 'what must soon come to pass,' of an angel sent to John, of a blessing on the one who reads and obeys, and of the near time. Revelation 22:6-10 repeats all of it, so that the book is closed with the same promise with which it began.

John falls at the angel's feet and is told, 'Worship God!' The same scene returns in 22:8-9 with almost the same words. The repetition shows how easy it is to bow to a messenger instead of the One who sent him, and how firmly the book keeps worship for God alone.

Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end. John is told in 22:10 not to seal his, because the time is near. The two commands hold the same prophetic story at different moments, and the open scroll of Revelation is the unsealing Daniel was waiting for.

Moses told Israel not to add to or subtract from what he commanded. Revelation 22:18-19 puts the same protection around this book, with plagues for adding and the loss of a share in the tree of life for taking away. The echo marks the book as God's word in the full sense.

Balaam saw a star come forth from Jacob and a scepter arise from Israel. Jesus calls Himself the bright Morning Star in 22:16, so that the oracle spoken to a pagan seer is gathered into the last words of the Bible and fulfilled in the person of the returning King.

A shoot springs up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots bears fruit. Isaiah 11:10 goes on to call Him the Root of Jesse, and Revelation 22:16 names Jesus 'the Root and the Offspring of David.' The Davidic king of the prophets is the Lord who speaks here.

'Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters' is the prophet's free invitation. Revelation 22:17 returns to it at the close of the Bible, 'let the one who desires the water of life drink freely,' and puts it in the mouth of the Spirit and the bride.

The Lord GOD comes with might, and 'His reward is with Him, and His recompense accompanies Him.' Jesus applies the language to Himself in Revelation 22:12, 'My reward is with Me,' which shows that the coming of Christ is the coming of the LORD of the prophets.

Paul ends his letter with 'Come, O Lord!', which is the Aramaic cry Maranatha rendered in English. It shows that the prayer of Revelation 22:20 was already the church's prayer in the earliest decades, spoken across languages as the last word of both a letter and a book.

Jesus asks how the Christ can be David's son if David calls Him 'Lord,' quoting Psalm 110:1. Revelation 22:16 supplies the answer, since He is both the Root and the Offspring of David, the source and the descendant, fully God and fully man.

The multitude have 'washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.' Revelation 22:14 uses the same image of washed robes for those who have the right to the tree of life, which shows that the washing in the epilogue is the cleansing the Lamb provides.

With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and He is patient, not wanting anyone to perish. It is the standard biblical answer to the question of why 'soon' has stretched across centuries: the delay is the space that mercy needs before the end.

study.oneStory:
The Bible began with a Word that made light, a garden, a tree of life and a man and woman who walked with God, and it ends here, with the Word of God sealed, the tree open and a people praying for the return of the Lord. This is the final movement of the story, and it answers the main questions the book has raised. How can a word that was twisted in Genesis 3, 'Did God really say?', be trusted again? By a God who is the Alpha and the Omega and who says that these words are faithful and true, and by a warning against altering them that protects the serpent's old method from being tried again. What of the curse? It was answered in 22:3, and in this section the way to the tree of life is stated as a blessing on the washed.

The passage also gathers the long line of promises. The star of Numbers, the Root of Isaiah, the Son of David, and the Lord who comes with His reward in Isaiah 40 and 62 are all one person, and He speaks as Jesus. The people who wait for Him are the people who were scattered at Babel and promised to Abraham as a blessing for all families of the earth, and in this section they are the bride and the thirsty, who are invited from every direction.

It sets up what remains, which is the present age of the church. The book does not end on the day of the return, and its last words are a prayer. Believers live between the promise and the coming with the Spirit, saying 'Come' and keeping the words. The story is complete in God's purpose, and yet it is still to be fully told. The old life of Eden is gone and the new life of the city is certain, and the church waits in grace.

Seen from the end, the Bible is one story with one Lord. It begins with God speaking and ends with God speaking, it begins with a barred tree and ends with an open one, and it begins with a question, 'Where are you?', in Genesis 3:9 and ends with an answer, 'Yes, I am coming soon.' The last word of the story is grace, and the last prayer is the church's, 'Come, Lord Jesus.'

sermon.title: Even So, Come, Lord Jesus!
sermon.why: Carson's sermon takes its title directly from this epilogue's closing prayer in 22:20 and preaches through Revelation 21:1-22:6, culminating in the church's response to Christ's promise, I am coming soon, with the ancient cry, Even so, come, Lord Jesus.

quiz.q: Why does the angel refuse John's worship in verses 8-9?

options.text: Because only God is to be worshiped; the angel is a fellow servant, not an object of worship.
options.note: The angel says plainly, 'Worship God!'

options.text: Because John had not properly prepared himself to worship.
options.note: The issue is who is worshiped, not John's readiness or preparation.

options.text: Because angels can never be honored in any way.
options.note: The angel is honored as a fellow servant; the objection is specifically to worship, which belongs to God alone.

options.text: Because the vision itself was false and unworthy of a response.
options.note: The angel has just called the words faithful and true; the correction concerns who receives worship, not the vision's truth.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' repeated statement, 'I am coming soon,' most likely convey?

options.text: The certainty and appropriate urgency of Christ's return, whether read as near in time or sudden once it begins.
options.note: Both major readings of 'soon' agree on certainty and the call to readiness.

options.text: A precise date that can be calculated from the surrounding text.
options.note: Revelation gives no calculable date; Acts 1:7 records Jesus refusing to disclose times or seasons.

options.text: That Christ had already returned by the time John wrote this.
options.note: The promise is future and repeated three times as still awaited.

options.text: That the promise of Christ's return no longer applies today.
options.note: The promise and the church's prayer for it remain live and repeated.

quiz.q: What is the warning in verses 18-19 about adding to or taking from the prophecy?

options.text: It echoes Deuteronomy's warning against tampering with God's word and guards the integrity of this book's message.
options.note: Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32 use nearly identical language.

options.text: It forbids anyone from ever reading the book of Revelation aloud.
options.note: The warning concerns altering the words, not reading or teaching them.

options.text: It applies only to scribes copying manuscripts in the ancient world.
options.note: While it addressed textual integrity then, its principle of guarding God's word carries ongoing weight.

options.text: It has no connection to any other part of Scripture.
options.note: It directly echoes the Deuteronomy warnings named above.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean calling Himself the Root and Offspring of David, the Morning Star, in verse 16?

options.text: That He is both David's divine source and his human descendant, and the star that fulfills ancient hope and heralds the dawn.
options.note: Root names His deity as David's source; Offspring names His true humanity as David's descendant.

options.text: That He was merely one more king in David's line, no different from the others.
options.note: The title Root sets Him above David as well as descended from him, unlike any other king in the line.

options.text: That He replaces David's line entirely with a new, unrelated dynasty.
options.note: He is explicitly David's own offspring, not a replacement for the line.

options.text: That the title has no connection to Old Testament promises.
options.note: It directly fulfills Numbers 24:17 and Isaiah 11:1, 10.

quiz.q: How does the church answer Christ's promise to come soon, in verses 17 and 20?

options.text: With the invitation and prayer, 'Come,' echoed by the Spirit, the bride, and every hearer, and finally addressed to Christ Himself.
options.note: This is the shape of verses 17 and 20, ending in 'Come, Lord Jesus.'

options.text: With silence, since no response to Christ's promise is recorded.
options.note: The text records an explicit, repeated response, 'Come.'

options.text: With a request that Christ delay His coming as long as possible.
options.note: The prayer asks for His coming, not for delay.

options.text: With a demand for proof before believing the promise.
options.note: The response is invitation and prayer, not demand or doubt.

questions: John, overwhelmed by the vision, tried to worship the angel rather than God. Where in your own life might awe or gratitude toward a person, gift, or experience be pulling your worship away from God alone?
Jesus says, 'Behold, I am coming soon,' three times in this chapter. Does that promise feel near and real to you, or distant? What would change if you lived today as though it were true?

The warning against adding to or taking from God's word is a serious one. Are there ways, even subtle ones, that you're tempted to add your own rules or subtract Christ's hard sayings from what Scripture actually teaches?
'Let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.' What is keeping you from coming freely to Christ today, rather than trying to earn or deserve His welcome?
The whole Bible ends with the prayer, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' and the blessing, 'grace to all the saints.' How might praying that prayer regularly change the way you face this season of waiting?

translationNotes.note: 'Coming soon' translates tachy, a word that in prophetic idiom can describe the suddenness and certainty of an event as much as its calendar nearness; readers differ on which sense is primary here, though both call for present readiness.

'Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End' stacks three near-synonymous titles of eternity together, underscoring by repetition Christ's total sovereignty over history rather than adding new information with each phrase.

The warning against adding to or taking away from 'the words of this book' closely echoes Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32's warnings about the Law, applied here to this specific prophetic book, and traditionally understood as bearing on the integrity of the whole of Scripture.

'Come, Lord Jesus' renders in Greek the same prayer 1 Corinthians 16:22 preserves in its original Aramaic, Maranatha, meaning 'our Lord, come' or 'our Lord has come,' one of the earliest recorded prayers of the church.
